objectives: Determine the shape of each scalar, vector, or matrix before carrying out addition, inner products, outer products, matrix multiplication, or element-wise multiplication, and explain what the result represents.
Use a determinant to decide whether a given two-by-two matrix is invertible, calculate its inverse by hand, and verify that the product is the identity matrix.
From a probability mass function or density, calculate normalization, means, variances, marginals, and conditional distributions, and distinguish “uncorrelated” from “independent.”
Derive Bayes' rule from the two factorizations of a joint probability and distinguish the prior, likelihood, evidence, and posterior clearly.
prerequisiteBridge: A vector can be understood first as an ordered column of numbers—for example, one neuron's responses under two conditions. A matrix is a table of numbers whose row and column meanings are preserved. Before calculating, write the shape beside every object: a column vector \(u\in \mathbb{R}^{2}\) is \(2\times 1\), while \(A\in \mathbb{R}^{4\times 2}\) is \(4\times 2\). The inner dimensions must match in matrix multiplication because each row of the left matrix forms an inner product with each column of the right object. The outer dimensions determine the answer's shape. This rule prevents more errors than memorizing isolated calculations.

Probability describes patterns of outcomes across repeated trials. A discrete variable uses sums of probabilities; a Bernoulli variable, for example, takes only 0 or 1. A continuous variable uses integrals of a density. Density at a point may exceed 1, but probability—the area over an interval—must lie between 0 and 1. The mean is the long-run average location, and variance is the mean squared distance from that location. Conditional probability restricts the sample space after information is known; it is not synonymous with causation.

MATLAB notation is not identical to mathematical notation: `*` performs matrix multiplication, `.*` multiplies corresponding elements, and an apostrophe transposes a real matrix. Software may permit implicit expansion between a scalar and matrix, but abstract matrix addition still requires matching shapes. Use three checks for every computation: write the shapes, predict a sign or order of magnitude, then verify an independent identity—for example, \(B\cdot B^{-1}\) should be close to the identity. Use the same discipline in probability: check normalization and range, then recompute by marginalization or a complementary event.

modules.title: Start with shape: scalars, vectors, matrices, and products
paragraphs: This section defines \(s=2\), \(u=(0,1)^{\mathrm{T}}\), \(v=(2,5)^{\mathrm{T}}\), \(w=(0,1,2,5)^{\mathrm{T}}\), and matrices A, B, and C. These are more than arithmetic exercises: a vector may represent responses from several neurons, and a matrix may represent a linear map from stimulus to response. Shape records the input and output slots. If you ignore it, you may swap neuron and condition indices even when the arithmetic itself is correct.

Vector addition requires equal lengths and proceeds component by component. The inner product \(u^{\mathrm{T}}v\) maps two equal-length vectors to a scalar and can measure overlap in a common coordinate system. The norm \(||w||_{2}\) is the square root of \(w^{\mathrm{T}}w\) and gives Euclidean distance from the origin. The outer product \(uv^{\mathrm{T}}\) maps two vectors to a matrix whose i,j entry is \(u_{i}\) \(v_{j}\), retaining every pairwise combination. Do not confuse it with the inner product.

Interpret Av as the inner product of each row of A with v. If A is \(4\times 2\) and v is \(2\times 1\), the result is \(4\times 1\), with each output component a weighted sum of two input components. Matrix product BC pairs every row of B with every column of C. Matrix multiplication is generally noncommutative: even when BC and CB have the same shape, they may have different values and represent transformations in different orders.

Keep the abstract rule separate from language behavior. In MATLAB, `B*C` is matrix multiplication and `B.*C` is element-wise multiplication; for a real vector, `v'` produces a row vector. Some versions permit s+A by implicitly adding the scalar to each entry. That is an array-language convention, not ordinary addition between linear-algebra objects of different shapes. State explicitly which meaning your code uses.
keyPoints: Matrix multiplication requires matching inner dimensions and retains the outer dimensions.
An inner product is a scalar; an outer product is a matrix. They retain different information.
Software implicit expansion must be distinguished conceptually from abstract matrix addition.

derivation.title: Calculate a specified matrix product from its entrywise definition
derivation.setup: Let \(A=[[0,0.5],[10,1],[2,9],[2,7]]\) and \(v=(2,5)^{\mathrm{T}}\). Calculate Av while tracking its shape.

steps.title: Check compatibility
steps.explanation: A is \(4\times 2\) and v is \(2\times 1\). The inner dimensions 2 match, so the product exists and has shape \(4\times 1\).

steps.title: Calculate the first two rows
steps.explanation: The first row gives \(0\cdot 2+0.5\cdot 5=2.5\), and the second gives \(10\cdot 2+1\cdot 5=25\).

steps.title: Calculate the last two rows
steps.explanation: The third row gives \(2\cdot 2+9\cdot 5=49\), and the fourth gives \(2\cdot 2+7\cdot 5=39\).

steps.title: Assemble and verify
steps.explanation: In row order, the result is the column vector \((2.5,25,49,39)^{\mathrm{T}}\). Its four outputs correspond one-to-one with the four rows of A.

symbolNotes: The columns of A correspond to two input features, and its rows correspond to four output channels.
The transpose symbol \(^{\mathrm{T}}\) converts a column vector into a row vector without changing component order.
derivation.unitsCheck: If A is dimensionless and every component of v has the same unit, Av has the same unit as v. If the two columns represent different physical quantities, their weights must carry the appropriate conversion units.
derivation.limitCheck: If \(v=0\), then Av must be the zero vector. If one row of A is entirely zero, the corresponding output must be zero.

workedExample.title: Distinguish the inner product, outer product, and norm
steps: The inner product is \(0\cdot 2+1\cdot 5=5\), a scalar.
The outer product is \([[0\cdot 2,0\cdot 5],[1\cdot 2,1\cdot 5]]=[[0,0],[2,5]]\), with shape \(2\times 2\).
workedExample.result: The sum is \((2,6)^{\mathrm{T}}\), the inner product is 5, the outer product is \([[0,0],[2,5]]\), and the norm is approximately 5.385.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The norm must exceed the largest component magnitude 5 and be smaller than the sum of component magnitudes 7; 5.385 satisfies both bounds.

pitfalls: Multiplying whenever two objects have the same number of entries, without checking the inner dimensions required by matrix multiplication.
Confusing `*` with `.*`, which can produce the expected shape but a different scientific meaning.

modules.title: Identity, transpose, inverse, and singularity
paragraphs: The identity matrix I has 1 on the diagonal and 0 elsewhere and plays the role of scalar 1: \(Ix=x\). Transpose \(A^{\mathrm{T}}\) swaps rows and columns. Thus, if A maps a two-dimensional input to a four-dimensional output, \(A^{\mathrm{T}}\) has shape \(2\times 4\), but it is generally not the inverse of A. An inverse \(A^{-1}\) must satisfy \(A^{-1}A=AA^{-1}=I\) and exists only for a square, one-to-one mapping.

For a two-by-two matrix \(B=[[a,b],[c,d]]\), \(\det(B)=ad-bc\). Geometrically, the determinant is the signed area scale factor of the linear map. A zero determinant means that a two-dimensional region is compressed into a line or point, so distinct inputs yield the same output. Once the map flattens information, output alone cannot identify the original input and no inverse exists. This is the same fact as linear dependence among rows or columns.

For \(B=[[4,4],[8,9]]\), \(\det(B)=36-32=4\), so \(B^{-1}=(1/4)[[9,-4],[-8,4]]\). Verification matters more than calling `inv`: multiplying by B should give 1 on the diagonal and 0 off the diagonal. In numerical work, a nonzero determinant that is very close to zero may still produce an inverse that amplifies tiny errors dramatically. Check the condition number instead of stopping at “the software returned an answer.”

The Hadamard product B⊙C multiplies corresponding entries and requires equal shapes; the matrix product BC sums along a shared index. The first may represent channel-wise gain, while the second composes transformations. Calling both simply “multiplication” erases model structure. In a code audit, describe the objects on both sides of every multiplication sign and verify the first entry by hand.
keyPoints: An inverse recovers the input uniquely from the output; a transpose does not serve that purpose.
A zero determinant means that a map compresses dimensions and loses recoverable information.
A Hadamard product is element-wise, whereas a matrix product sums over the shared dimension.

derivation.title: The two-by-two inverse formula and numerical verification
derivation.setup: Find the inverse of \(B=[[4,4],[8,9]]\) and verify it by multiplying in both orders.

steps.title: Calculate the determinant
steps.explanation: \(\det(B)=4\cdot 9-4\cdot 8=4\). Because it is nonzero, the inverse exists.

steps.title: Swap and negate
steps.explanation: For a two-by-two inverse, swap the main-diagonal entries, negate the off-diagonal entries, and divide by the determinant.

steps.title: Check the first row
steps.explanation: In \(B\cdot B^{-1}\), the first-row, first-column entry is \((4\cdot 9+4\cdot (-8))/4=1\). For the first-row, second-column entry, the two numerator terms are \(4\cdot (-4)\) and \(4\cdot 4\); after division by 4, the result is 0.

steps.title: Check the second row
steps.explanation: The second-row, first-column entry is \((8\cdot 9+9\cdot (-8))/4=0\), and the second-row, second-column entry is \((8\cdot (-4)+9\cdot 4)/4=1\), giving I.

symbolNotes: \(\det(B)\) is a scalar, and \(B^{-1}\) has the same shape as B.
The denominator \(\det(B)\) explains why the formula fails when the determinant is zero.
derivation.unitsCheck: If B maps units X to units Y, its entries carry Y/X and \(B^{-1}\) carries X/Y; their dimensionless product is I.
derivation.limitCheck: As the second row approaches a constant multiple of the first, \(\det(B)\) approaches zero, inverse entries grow in magnitude, and small observational errors are amplified.

workedExample.title: Compare matrix and element-wise multiplication
steps: The first row of BC is \(4\cdot 3+4\cdot 6=36\) and \(4\cdot 4+4\cdot 8=48\).
Both results have shape \(2\times 2\), but the first composes linear transformations while the second weights corresponding positions.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Every entry of BC is a sum of two products; every Hadamard entry is one product of corresponding elements.

pitfalls: Treating a nonzero determinant as sufficient for numerical stability and ignoring error amplification near singularity.
Using `inv(B)*y` instead of a more stable linear solve and failing to verify the result.

modules.title: From Bernoulli and exponential distributions to joint Gaussians and Bayes
paragraphs: A Bernoulli variable X takes only 1 or 0 with probabilities p and 1−p. Its mean is \(E[X]=p\) because \(1\cdot p+0\cdot (1-p)=p\). Since \(X^{2}=X\), its variance is \(E[X^{2}]-E[X]^{2}=p-p^{2}=p(1-p)\). This can represent whether a spike occurs in a time window or whether a choice is correct. Counts across multiple windows form a binomial distribution only if trials are independent and share the same p.

The exponential density \(f(x)=\lambda \exp(-\lambda x)\), \(x\ge 0\), describes waiting times in a constant-rate Poisson process. Integration gives \(F(x)=1-\exp(-\lambda x)\), so the survival probability is \(\exp(-\lambda x)\). The mean and standard deviation are both \(1/\lambda\), the median is \(\ln 2/\lambda\), and the mode is 0. A mean larger than the median reflects the long right tail. Treating \(\lambda\) as the mean waiting time gives both a dimensional and numerical error.

A bivariate Gaussian is determined completely by its mean vector and covariance matrix. Integrating out one variable gives a Gaussian marginal; fixing an observation and renormalizing gives a Gaussian conditional distribution. Conditioning shifts the mean and reduces variance to the uncertainty left after accounting for the correlation. The derivation below gives the conditional mean, conditional variance, and Bayesian reweighting, allowing you to calculate the complete distribution rather than merely infer the tilt of an ellipse.

Bayes' rule follows from two factorizations of one joint probability: \(P(A,B)=P(A|B)P(B)=P(B|A)P(A)\). Rearrangement gives \(P(A|B)=P(B|A)P(A)/P(B)\). In parameter inference, A may be parameter \(\theta\) and B the data D. Then \(P(D|\theta )\) is the likelihood, \(P(\theta )\) the prior, \(P(D)\) the normalizing evidence, and \(P(\theta |D)\) the posterior. A likelihood is not a probability distribution over the parameter unless it is multiplied by a prior and normalized.
keyPoints: Bernoulli variance \(p(1-p)\) is zero at \(p=0\) or 1 and maximal at \(p=1/2\).
Exponential rate \(\lambda\) and mean waiting time \(1/\lambda\) are reciprocals.
For jointly Gaussian variables, zero covariance implies independence; general distributions do not share this guarantee.
Bayes' rule is a rearrangement of two factorizations of the joint probability.

derivation.title: From conditioning a bivariate Gaussian to Bayesian reweighting
derivation.setup: Let \((X_{1},X_{2})\) be jointly Gaussian with mean \((\mu _{1},\mu _{2})\), standard deviations \(\sigma _{1}\) and \(\sigma _{2}\), correlation c, and \(|c|<1\). First obtain the full distribution of \(X_{1}|X_{2}=x_{2}\), then connect this continuous conditioning problem to Bayes' rule.

steps.title: Write the mean and covariance
steps.explanation: Diagonal entries are variances, while each off-diagonal entry is the correlation coefficient times both standard deviations.

steps.title: Calculate the determinant and inverse
steps.explanation: The factor \(1-c^{2}\) in the determinant determines whether the covariance is degenerate. The negative off-diagonal entries of the bivariate inverse create the conditional-mean correction when the Gaussian exponent is completed to a square.

steps.title: Marginalize first
steps.explanation: Integrating over the full range of \(x_{1}\) removes that dimension. The marginal of a bivariate Gaussian remains a univariate Gaussian with \(\operatorname{mean} \mu _{2}\) and variance \(\sigma _{2}^{2}\).

steps.title: Take a slice at the observed value
steps.explanation: Fix \(X_{2}=x_{2}\) in the joint density and absorb every factor depending only on \(x_{2}\) into the normalizing constant. The remaining exponent in \(x_{1}\) is still quadratic.

steps.title: Complete the square to obtain the conditional mean
steps.explanation: Completing the square in \(x_{1}\) shifts the center along the correlation direction. With positive correlation and \(x_{2}\) below its own mean, the conditional mean also shifts downward.

steps.title: Read off the conditional variance
steps.explanation: The quadratic term after completing the square gives the remaining variance. Knowing \(X_{2}\) reduces uncertainty from \(\sigma _{1}^{2}\) to \(\sigma _{1}^{2}(1-c^{2})\).

steps.title: Write the full conditional distribution
steps.explanation: A one-dimensional Gaussian requires both a mean and a variance; the conditional distribution is incomplete unless both are stated.

steps.title: Connect to Bayes' rule
steps.explanation: Both continuous densities and discrete probabilities update by conditioning through two factorizations of the same joint quantity. The denominator is the evidence obtained by summing or integrating over every candidate cause.

symbolNotes: c is the correlation coefficient. A nondegenerate bivariate Gaussian requires \(|c|<1\); when \(c=0\), the variables are independent.
\(\mu _{1}|_{2}\) is the conditional mean after observing a specific \(x_{2}\), and \(\sigma _{1}|_{2}^{2}\) is the conditional variance. Report both.
The Bayesian denominator \(P(B)\), or \(p(x_{2})\), renormalizes the result. The continuous case uses densities rather than point probabilities.
derivation.unitsCheck: c is dimensionless. Multiplying \(\sigma _{1}/\sigma _{2}\) by \((x_{2}-\mu _{2})\) yields units of \(X_{1}\). Conditional variance and \(\sigma _{1}^{2}\) both have squared \(X_{1}\) units. Normalization preserves the appropriate units for probabilities and probability densities.
derivation.limitCheck: When \(c=0\), the conditional mean returns to \(\mu _{1}\) and the conditional variance to \(\sigma _{1}^{2}\). As \(|c|\to 1\), the nondegenerate model approaches a line, conditional variance approaches zero, and the covariance matrix becomes singular.

workedExample.title: Two normalizations: a conditional Gaussian and low-base-rate Bayes
workedExample.problem: A: \(\mu _{1}=0\), \(\mu _{2}=1\), \(\sigma _{1}=0.5\), \(\sigma _{2}=1\), \(c=0.7\), and \(x_{2}=0.75\). Find the conditional mean, variance, and standard deviation of \(X_{1}\). B: disease prevalence is 1%, sensitivity is 0.9, and false-positive rate is 0.05. Find the probability of disease after a positive result.
steps: For A, the conditional mean is \(0+0.7\cdot 0.5\cdot (0.75-1)=-0.0875\).
The conditional variance is \(0.5^{2}(1-0.7^{2})=0.25\cdot 0.51=0.1275\), so the conditional standard deviation is approximately 0.3571.
Because correlation is positive and \(x_{2}\) is below \(\mu _{2}\), the conditional mean falls below \(\mu _{1}\). The conditional variance 0.1275 is also smaller than the marginal variance 0.25.
For B, the joint probability of a true positive is \(0.9\cdot 0.01=0.009\), and that of a false positive is \(0.05\cdot 0.99=0.0495\).
The total probability of a positive result is \(0.009+0.0495=0.0585\).
The posterior probability after a positive result is \(0.009/0.0585\approx 0.1538\), or about 15.4%.
workedExample.result: A: conditional mean −0.0875, variance 0.1275, and standard deviation about 0.357. B: probability of disease after a positive result about 15.4%.
workedExample.sanityCheck: In A, the mean moves in the direction implied by the observation and conditional uncertainty decreases. In B, the posterior exceeds the 1% prior but remains far below the 90% sensitivity.

pitfalls: Treating a continuous density \(f(x)\) as a point probability \(P(X=x)\), even though probability comes from integration over an interval.
Confusing \(P(A|B)\) with \(P(B|A)\), especially by ignoring the prior in a low-base-rate setting.
Generalizing zero correlation to independence for arbitrary distributions.
